title: Parenting Basics
summary: Practical, evidence-based parenting: how children develop, connection and communication, positive discipline and tantrums, health, nutrition and home safety, learning, play and screen time, and caring for yourself and protecting children.
audience: Parents, expecting parents, grandparents, guardians and caregivers

body.p: Parenting is the work of raising children to be healthy, safe, capable and kind. Every parent and caregiver, including grandparents, older siblings and guardians, can learn skills that make it easier. Children develop physically, mentally, emotionally and socially, and each stage brings new needs.

list: Infants (0 to 1 year): rapid brain growth; they need warmth, feeding, sleep and responsive care. Talking, singing and smiling with babies builds language and trust.
Toddlers (1 to 3 years): walking, first words and a strong drive for independence; tantrums are a normal sign they cannot yet manage big feelings.
Pre-school (3 to 5 years): imagination, play, questions and early friendships.
School age (6 to 12 years): learning, skills, rules and fairness matter; friendships grow in importance.
Teenagers (13 to 19 years): physical changes, a search for identity, more independence and peer influence; they still need guidance and connection.

body.p: The early years, especially the first 1000 days from pregnancy to age two, are especially important for brain development, nutrition and lifelong health.

body.tip: Children develop at different speeds; talk to a health worker if you are worried about speech, movement or behaviour milestones.

body.p: A warm, secure relationship with at least one caring adult is one of the strongest protections a child can have. It helps children cope with stress, learn better and form healthy relationships later.

list: Spend one-on-one time each day, even five minutes of full attention, following the child's lead in play or conversation.
Listen without rushing to judge or fix; ask about their day with open questions.
Praise effort and specific behaviour ("You kept trying with that puzzle") rather than only results.
Name feelings: "You look disappointed that the game ended." This helps children understand and manage emotions.
Show affection with hugs, kind words and attention, in ways that suit your family and culture.

body.p: Teenagers often talk more during side-by-side activities, such as cooking, walking or driving, than face to face. Stay calm when they share difficult things, so they keep coming to you.

body.tip: Put phones away during meals and conversations; children notice where your attention goes.

body.p: Discipline means teaching, not punishing. Positive discipline helps children learn self-control and good behaviour while keeping the relationship strong. Research shows that harsh physical punishment is linked to worse behaviour, anxiety and aggression over time, and many African countries have laws against corporal punishment of children.

list: Set clear, simple rules and explain the reasons.
Give positive instructions: "Walk, please" rather than "Don't run".
Be consistent: the same behaviour should lead to the same response.
Use natural and logical consequences: if a toy is thrown, it is put away for a while.
Catch them being good and praise it; attention increases behaviours.
Use calm time-outs or a pause for big emotions, for both child and parent.

body.p: Stay calm, keep the child safe, and wait for the storm to pass before talking. Then name the feeling and teach a better way to express it. Giving in to tantrums teaches children that tantrums work.

body.tip: Plan for difficult moments, such as shopping or bedtime, by explaining what will happen and offering simple choices.

list: Follow the national immunisation schedule; vaccines protect against measles, polio, whooping cough and other dangerous diseases.
Breastfeeding: health authorities such as the WHO recommend exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, then continued breastfeeding with suitable foods.
Offer a varied diet with vegetables, fruits, proteins and whole grains, and limit sugary drinks and snacks.
Ensure enough sleep: children need more sleep than adults, and routines help.
Wash hands with soap, use safe drinking water and keep the home clean to prevent diarrhoea and infections.

body.p: Keep medicines, cleaning products and paraffin out of reach, preferably locked away and never in drink bottles. Supervise children near water, including buckets and pools, as young children can drown in a few centimetres of water. Keep hot liquids and fires away from children, and use proper car seats or seat belts.

body.tip: Seek medical help quickly for danger signs in children, such as difficulty breathing, convulsions, inability to drink or extreme drowsiness.

body.p: Play is how children learn. Through play they develop language, problem-solving, creativity, physical skills and social skills.

list: Read or tell stories every day, in any language; it builds vocabulary and a love of learning.
Provide simple materials: blocks, boxes, crayons, sand and water. Expensive toys are not necessary.
Involve children in daily tasks such as cooking, counting money or gardening.
Show interest in schoolwork, talk with teachers and create a regular homework time and place.

body.p: The WHO advises no screen time for babies under one, and no more than one hour a day for children aged two to four, with less being better. For older children, set limits, keep devices out of bedrooms at night, choose good-quality content, and talk about online safety: not sharing personal information and telling an adult if something online upsets them.

body.tip: Model the habits you want: children copy what adults do more than what adults say.

lessons.title: Caring for yourself and getting support

body.p: Parenting is demanding, and stressed, exhausted parents find it harder to be patient. Caring for yourself is part of caring for your children.

list: Rest when you can, eat well and keep up friendships.
Share responsibilities with partners, family and trusted friends; it takes a village to raise a child.
Join parenting groups at clinics, schools, churches or mosques to share experiences.
Notice signs of depression, such as persistent sadness or loss of interest, which can affect parents, including after birth, and seek help from a health worker.
Repair after mistakes: apologising to your child teaches them how to handle conflict.

body.p: Teach children the correct names for body parts, that their body belongs to them, and that they can tell you about anything that makes them uncomfortable without being blamed. Know who your children spend time with. If you suspect a child is being harmed, contact child protection services, the police or a child helpline in your country.

body.tip: Three moments of connection a day, such as morning, after school and bedtime, of even 20 minutes in total, make a lasting difference.
